title: Sparse-context multiplexing microbench — lab scratch
content:
Goal:
Short notes for an exploratory microbenchmark: understand how KV-cache eviction + multiplexing interacts with a mixed workload that mixes lots of short requests with occasional long-context sessions. Trying to reproduce weird p99 spikes seen in prod when short QPS and long chat sessions coincide.

Motivation / quick background:
- Prod telemetry shows occasional ~2-3x p99 increase when a few long-context sessions (>= 2k tokens) overlap with a background of short single-turn QPS. Suspect cache churn + batching heuristics are compounding.
- Want to measure: (1) p50/p95/p99 for short requests, (2) tail amplification for long sessions, (3) effect of KV cache size + eviction policy and multiplexing window.

Hypotheses:
1) When short requests are interleaved with long context sessions, continuous batching coalesces requests and pushes the long request into the same batch, expanding per-token latency and hurting tails.
2) KV cache thrash: long sessions fill the KV cache and evict prefixes used by short requests; re-computation penalties increase tail.
3) Small changes to multiplexer fairness (short-pref bias) or eviction watermarks reduce short-request p99 with minimal throughput loss.

Experiment setup (single node microbench):
- Model: redwood-open-7B-qlora (approx 7B) in fp16 (baseline) + quantized run (int8) for one sweep.
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB (single GPU).
- Runtime: local debug build from PR-884 (see linked), with instrumentation enabled for batch composition and KV metrics.
- Client generator: custom harness that supports mixing arrival processes.
- Arrival mix: 70% short (prompt length 16 tokens, gen length 8), 25% medium (prompt 128, gen 64), 5% long-session (initial prompt 800 tokens then 4 incremental continuations of 400 tokens each arriving every 2s).
- Concurrency: target steady QPS=240 short-equivalent (measured), ramp to steady over 30s.
- Run length: 12 minutes per trial (enough to let long sessions progress and produce eviction churn).
- Cache config variants: KV cache sizes = [2GB, 8GB, 24GB], eviction policy = [LRU, segmented-LRU], multiplexer fairness = [fair, short-pref].

Commands & flags (notes):
- harness: ./bench --model redwood-open-7B --arrival-config mix.yaml --qps 240 --duration 720 --log-batches
- runtime flags toggled: --kv-cache-max-bytes, --eviction-policy, --multiplexer-window-ms, --prefer-short-requests

Collected metrics (per trial):
- p50/p95/p99 latencies for short requests
- average batch size and fraction of batches containing a long request
- KV cache hit rate by token position (prefix vs suffix)
- tail amplification factor = p99_short_with_long / p99_short_baseline
- throughput (tokens/s) and GPU util

Representative results (raw numbers simplified):
Trial A: KV=2GB, LRU, fair mux
- short p50=12ms, p95=45ms, p99=210ms
- batch avg size=6, batches_with_long=0.12
- kv-hit(short-prefix)=0.63
- tail amplification factor ~2.1

Trial B: KV=8GB, seg-LRU, fair mux
- short p50=11ms, p95=38ms, p99=120ms
- batch avg size=5.4, batches_with_long=0.09
- kv-hit(short-prefix)=0.81
- tail amp ~1.2

Trial C: KV=8GB, seg-LRU, short-pref mux
- short p50=10ms, p95=32ms, p99=65ms
- batch avg size=4.1, batches_with_long=0.04
- kv-hit(short-prefix)=0.85
- tail amp ~0.7 (i.e., short latency improved compared to baseline)

Trial D: KV=24GB, seg-LRU, fair mux (quantized model)
- short p50=14ms, p95=52ms, p99=140ms
- batch avg size=6.8, batches_with_long=0.15
- kv-hit(short-prefix)=0.79
- note: quantized run had higher variance in p95 but lower tokens/s cost.

Observations / quick interpretation:
- Small KV caches (2GB) cannot hold active prefixes from medium+long sessions; short requests suffer as their prefixes keep getting evicted -> re-encode penalty observed.
- Multiplexer fairness has outsized impact: biasing towards short requests significantly reduces batch coalescing with long requests, lowering tail for shorts with small throughput drop.
- Segmented-LRU (seg-LRU) stabilizes hit-rate for short prefixes compared to plain LRU. Suggests segregating short vs long prefix sets.
- Quantization reduces per-token compute but can increase latency variance; when combined with poor mux policies it can worsen tails.

Oddities / anomalies to follow up:
- In Trial B we observed occasional ~800ms outliers for short requests even when batches_with_long was <0.1. Correlated with GC-like memcpy spikes in the runtime; need more tracing (nvprof + heap snapshots).
- When running medium-heavy mix (50% medium) the effectiveness of short-pref mux reduces; need to tune threshold heuristics for what counts as "short".

Actionable next steps:
1) Add a small in-process metric that tags batches containing any request with context > 256 tokens and expose that in tracing to correlate tails with specific batches.
2) Prototype a two-bucket KV cache (short-prefix bucket, long-session bucket) and run 3 quick trials (2GB, 8GB, 24GB split ratios 70/30 vs 50/50).
3) Reproduce Trial B anomaly with gdb+heap profiler + nvprof to see if memcpy/GPU memcpy contention corresponds to spikes.
4) Add a simple multiplexer knob: max_batch_tokens cap to prevent a single long request from expanding batch token budget. Measure impact.
5) Discuss with Lina about adding a small per-tenant priority hint at ingress (shortPriority) to bias mux early.

Notes-to-self (short checklist):
- [ ] instrument batch traces with per-request context-length and kv-cache-eviction-id
- [ ] add flag --max-batch-token-cap and test at 2048 tokens
- [ ] re-run quantized trials with pinned CPU memory to rule out page faults
- [ ] sync with runtime team next Tue (Arjun & Lina) to align eviction policy experiments

Raw logs / pointers:
- run IDs: run-20241103-01A, run-20241103-01B, run-20241103-02Q
- small plot sketches saved in /tmp/sparse-mux-plots (pngs)

Loose conclusions for the notebook:
- For mixed short/long workloads, prefer small structural changes: short-pref mux + seg-LRU + modest KV (8GB) gives best p99 reduction for short requests without hurting throughput materially.
- Quantization helps cost but requires careful variance testing; not a silver bullet for tail problems.

This doc is a scratchpad. Will extract a tidy playbook if follow-ups corroborate.
